title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM DIOTREPHES
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM DIOTREPHES
There are names in Scripture that are remembered because they loved God.
There are names remembered because they suffered for God.
There are names remembered because they changed the world.
And then there is Diotrephes.
A man mentioned only once in the Bible.
A man who occupies just a few verses.
A man with no recorded miracles.
No sermons.
No victories.
No great acts of faith.
Yet two thousand years later, believers still speak his name.
Not because he built God's Kingdom.
But because he tried to build his own.
That should make every one of us pause.
Because Diotrephes is not merely a man from the first century.
Diotrephes is a warning.
He is a mirror.
And if we are honest, many of us have seen pieces of him staring back at us.
The Apostle John writes:
(3 John 9)
The phrase "loveth to have the preeminence" comes from the Greek word φιλοπρωτεύων (philoprōteuōn).
It means "one who loves being first."
One who desires prominence.
One who craves superiority.
One who seeks recognition above others.
John does not begin by attacking Diotrephes' doctrine.
He begins by exposing his heart.
Because pride usually appears long before false teaching does.
The greatest danger in ministry is not always heresy.
Sometimes it is ego wearing a ministry badge.
Sometimes it is ambition dressed in spiritual language.
Sometimes it is a desire to be seen, applauded, followed, and admired.
The tragedy is that pride can hide behind religious activity.
A person can speak about Jesus while secretly wanting people to notice them instead.
A person can lead worship while worshipping their own importance.
A person can preach Christ while building a personal kingdom.
Diotrephes was not remembered because he denied Jesus.
He was remembered because he loved himself too much.
John continues:
"Neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church."
(3 John 10)
The evidence of pride is often seen in how we treat people.
Diotrephes was not content merely to elevate himself.
He pushed others down.
He rejected faithful believers.
He resisted apostolic authority.
He controlled access.
He silenced opposition.
He weaponized influence.
He used spiritual power for personal gain.
And history has repeated that pattern countless times.
Whenever leaders become more concerned about protecting their position than serving God's people, the spirit of Diotrephes is present.
Whenever churches revolve around personalities instead of Christ, the spirit of Diotrephes is present.
Whenever believers compete instead of serve, the spirit of Diotrephes is present.
Whenever recognition becomes more important than faithfulness, the spirit of Diotrephes is present.
Yet before we point fingers at church leaders, we should look inward.
Because Diotrephes is not merely a leadership problem.
He is a human problem.
The desire to be first lives in every fallen heart.
It appears in marriages.
Friendships.
Workplaces.
Churches.
Families.
Social media.
We want credit.
Recognition.
Validation.
Importance.
Influence.
Significance.
We want our opinions heard.
Our sacrifices noticed.
Our contributions acknowledged.
The flesh loves a throne.
But Jesus teaches a radically different way.
When the disciples argued about greatness, Jesus did not congratulate their ambition.
He confronted it.
In Mark 10:43-45 He said:
"Whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister."
The Greek word διάκονος (diakonos) means servant.
Not celebrity.
Not ruler.
Not master.
Servant.
And then Jesus pointed to Himself as the ultimate example.
"The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."
The King became a servant.
The Creator washed feet.
The Lord carried a cross.
The One who deserved everything surrendered everything.
This is the Gospel.
The world says climb higher.
Jesus says kneel lower.
The world says demand recognition.
Jesus says serve faithfully.
The world says become great.
Jesus says become humble.
Perhaps that is why one of the most beautiful words in Scripture is found in Philippians 2.
The Greek word is κένωσις (kenōsis).
It describes Christ emptying Himself.
Not of deity.
But of privilege.
He willingly embraced humility.
He willingly embraced sacrifice.
He willingly embraced suffering.
And because He humbled Himself, God highly exalted Him.
The path upward in God's Kingdom always begins downward.
That truth transformed how I see Diotrephes.
Because I realized something uncomfortable.
The greatest threat to my ministry is not opposition.
It is pride.
The greatest threat to my walk with God is not persecution.
It is self-exaltation.
The greatest threat to my spiritual life is not what others think about me.
It is what I secretly think about myself.
Pride is dangerous because it can survive success.
It can survive applause.
It can survive ministry growth.
It can survive religious activity.
It can sit quietly in a church pew while convincing us we are more spiritual than everyone else.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly warn against this danger.
Proverbs 16:18 declares:
"Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall."
The Hebrew word for pride here is גָּאוֹן (ga'on).
It carries the idea of arrogance, self-exaltation, and inflated importance.
The lesson is timeless.
Whenever we elevate ourselves, we place ourselves in danger.
Because God opposes pride but gives grace to the humble.
And that is where the story shifts.
Because the Bible is not merely a story about proud people.
It is a story about a gracious Savior.
Diotrephes reminds us of what pride can become.
Jesus reminds us of what grace can do.
Peter was proud.
Yet grace restored him.
Paul was proud.
Yet grace transformed him.
The prodigal son was proud.
Yet grace welcomed him home.
Every believer who has ever walked with Christ has fought the battle against pride.
The difference is not perfection.
The difference is repentance.
The Gospel does not call us to pretend pride does not exist.
The Gospel calls us to bring it into the light.
To confess it.
To crucify it.
To surrender it.
To let Christ replace our hunger for recognition with a hunger for His glory.
Perhaps that is why the Aramaic cry of the early church remains so powerful:
ܡܪܢ ܐܬܐ (Maranatha)
"Our Lord comes."
When Christ returns, earthly fame will mean nothing.
Titles will mean nothing.
Platforms will mean nothing.
Followers will mean nothing.
Only faithfulness will matter.
Only obedience will matter.
Only Christ will matter.
And on that day, nobody will regret being too humble.
Nobody will regret serving too much.
Nobody will regret loving too deeply.
Nobody will regret making Jesus the center instead of themselves.
The lesson I learned from Diotrephes is simple.
Never build a throne where God intended a cross.
Never seek prominence when Christ calls you to service.
Never pursue your own glory when Jesus deserves all glory.
Because the story of Diotrephes is ultimately a warning.
But the story of Jesus is an invitation.
An invitation away from pride.
Away from self-promotion.
Away from self-worship.
And into the freedom of humility.
Into the joy of surrender.
Into the beauty of grace.
If this article exposed an area where pride has quietly been growing, do not ignore what the Holy Spirit may be revealing.
Be honest. This may have hit closer than expected.
Someone you know may need this reminder today.
One day every platform will fade, every title will disappear, and every applause will fall silent—but the souls touched for Jesus Christ will remain forever.
